new_statements.quote: p.36: "3.1.5 Tone in Ɔkere. Like most Kwa languages, Ɔkere is a tone language. It has two level tones, that is, high (H) and low (L) as in kɛ ‘to show’ and ky ‘building’. The two level tones combine to give falling and rising tones as in h ‘to blow’. Grammatical and lexical functions are determined by tone." [tone-marked vowels of the example words are dropped in the repository's text layer] — p.131: "As a tone language, tone is crucial in most situations in the language. Ɔkere has two level tones, that is, high (H) and low (L). Tone has both grammatical and lexical functions."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ɔkere (Cherepon) is described as a tone language with two level tones (H, L) combining into falling and rising contours, with lexical minimal pairs (àkyí 'lady' / ákyì 'knife', Oppong 2019:8) and grammatical tone (bé NEG vs bè FUT; H-tone completive). Neither Animah 2015 nor Oppong 2019 says anything about word stress or accent placement; no accessible source makes a stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding prominence; only tonal alternations (NEG/FUT on be, completive H tone, H tone on nominalized/fronted forms) are described.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical items in citation form and short clauses; the phonology is a brief sketch inside a syntax thesis (fieldwork in Abiriw/Adukrom area). Oppong 2019 §1.5.1 p.8 independently repeats: 'Tone is contrastive in Ɔkere, with two contrastive tones in the language (Animah 2015).'
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe Ɔkere (= Okere = Kyerepong = Cherepon, ISO cpn, Glottolog cher1271) as spoken in Abiriw, Adukrom, Dawu, Awukugua, Apirede, Abonse and Aseseeso (Okere/Akuapem North, Eastern Region, Ghana); Animah 2015 and Oppong 2019 use data mainly from Abiriw and Adukrom. PHOIBLE's 'Hill Guang (GM 1323)' inventory is filed under cher1271 but its source (Painter 1980) is a Hill Guang data sheet that may pool Cherepon with Larteh (lart1238) and Gua/Anum-Boso (guaa1234).

sources.note: Ch.3 'A sketch grammar', §3.1 phonology (vowels, consonants, ATR harmony) and §3.1.5 'Tone in Ɔkere' (p.36): Ɔkere is a tone language with two level tones H and L that combine into falling/rising contours; tone has lexical and grammatical functions (e.g. bé NEG vs bè FUT; completive marked by H tone). Repeated p.131. No mention of word stress or accent anywhere in the thesis.

sources.citation: Asinyor, E., Owusu, E., Adade-Yeboah, A. & Dansieh, S.A. 2020. A Comparative Study of the Simple Clause Structure of Kyerepong (Okere), Akuapem Twi, and English. International Journal of Language & Linguistics 7(4):100-110. doi:10.30845/ijll.v7n4p13
sources.note: Only 'phonological processes' in clause formation: notes high tone transferring to a preceding syllable when a pronoun fuses with the perfect marker; 'stress' is discussed only for English focus. No Kyerepong word-stress statement. Cites Bramson 1981 (UG thesis on Kyerepong varieties).
